span.label: how single neurons in the human medial temporal lobe represent concepts, and how that representation behaves as a stimulus is repeated
span.quote: We also present key characteristics of the so-called ‘concept cells’, neurons in the human medial temporal lobe with selective and invariant responses that represent the meaning of the stimulus, and discuss their proposed role in declarative memory.

span.label: whether the response of a concept cell decays to baseline with repetition or settles at a stable level above it
span.quote: The screening data used in the study of Pedreira and colleagues had only six presentations of the stimuli. Although a response modulation with stimulus repetition was evident, the stability of these representations over several trials could not be addressed, as it was hard to see a steady state in the response strength. Therefore, the question of whether the response would end up reaching a baseline level after a sufficient number of repetitions remained open.

span.label: after an initial decay the response reaches an asymptote above baseline at about 15 presentations and stays there for the rest of the session
span.quote: Finally, we present novel results dealing with the stability of the representation given by these neurons, by studying the effect of stimulus repetition in the strength of the responses. In particular, we show that, after an initial decay, the response strength reaches an asymptotic value after approximately 15 presentations that remains above baseline for the whole duration of the experiment.

span.label: existence
span.quote: In particular, we show that, after an initial decay, the response strength reaches an asymptotic value after approximately 15 presentations that remains above baseline for the whole duration of the experiment.

span.label: concept cells in the human medial temporal lobe
span.quote: We also present novel results dealing with the stability of the responses of concept cells, using a visual paradigm where each stimulus was shown between 20 and 30 times.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: The data we present in this study, both for illustrating single-cell responses and for studying the stability of these responses, were collected using commercially available (Ad-Tech) depth electrodes, where each bundle had eight active microwires and one low-impedance microwire that was used as local reference.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: The loss of relevance may then diminish the size of the cell assembly encoding the concept, and this may constitute a key neural mechanism of forgetting

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: Using this classification, it was reported that MTL interneurons tend to fire to a larger number of stimuli, a finding that suggests a winner-takes-all mechanism that (by suppressing the firing of other neurons) may generate the very selective responses of pyramidal cells

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: The activity of these neurons decayed with trial number, resembling the repetition suppression effect found in monkeys, and it was argued that this pattern of responses may reflect the decrease of relevant information to be stored into memory after each presentation

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: Sensory stimuli related to this concept, such as a picture or the written or spoken name of a person, would then activate different subsets of the assembly, which in turn activate the whole assembly via pattern completion

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: This theta phase locking was proposed to reflect a global activation that provides a temporal window for the processing of consciously perceived stimuli in the MTL.

span.label: sparse coding: a concept is carried by a small assembly whose members respond explicitly to it and stay silent otherwise
span.quote: Because these neurons fire to relatively very few stimuli, each stimulus is likely to be encoded by a relatively small neuronal assembly (Quian Quiroga et al. 2008a ). In this ‘sparse coding’ view, the members of the assembly respond in an explicit manner to the specific concept they encode and typically remain silent for other objects.

span.label: interneurons fire to more stimuli than pyramidal cells, suggesting a winner-take-all step that sharpens the selective responses
span.quote: First of all, on the basis of their spike widths and firing rates it is in principle possible to classify neurons as interneurons or pyramidal cells. Using this classification, it was reported that MTL interneurons tend to fire to a larger number of stimuli, a finding that suggests a winner-takes-all mechanism that (by suppressing the firing of other neurons) may generate the very selective responses of pyramidal cells

span.label: the more personally relevant a stimulus, the larger the assembly encoding it
span.quote: In line, it has been shown that pictures of family members, including pictures of the patients themselves (see Fig. 4b ), and pictures of the researchers performing experiments with the patients, who are in close contact with them throughout their stay in hospital, are the most likely to elicit responses, followed by pictures of celebrities, and then by pictures of unfamiliar faces (Viskontas et al. 2009 ). In other words, we can infer that the more personally relevant the stimulus, the larger the number of neurons encoding it.

span.label: loss of relevance may shrink the assembly, which is proposed as a mechanism of forgetting
span.quote: Following these arguments, we can hypothesize that the stable representation by concept cells might last for as long as the concept remains relevant. The loss of relevance may then diminish the size of the cell assembly encoding the concept, and this may constitute a key neural mechanism of forgetting

span.label: strong responses on the very first presentation imply the concept was already encoded before the experiment, since a temporary assignment would have needed several trials to form
span.quote: In particular, the screening sessions used in Pedreira et al. ( 2010 ) were the very first experiments done with the patients, so the first trial corresponds to the very first presentation of each stimulus. Given the strong responses found from the first trial, we can infer that concept cells were involved in the encoding of the concept (which had not necessarily been active in the recent past) before the experiment took place. In fact, a non-stable, temporary representation of concepts would have implied a reassignment of these concepts to random sets of neurons after the first presentation, which would have taken at least a few trials to establish.

span.label: A further decay beyond the ~30 repetitions tested cannot be excluded.
span.quote: Although we cannot rule out a further decrease after many more repetitions, it seems that concept cells continue responding to a stimulus above baseline.

span.label: The published estimates of how many neurons encode a concept are only upper bounds, given personally relevant images, ~100 pictures and ~30-min sessions.
span.quote: As a matter of fact, these estimates should only be considered as upper bounds

span.label: Neurons that fired to a single concept might have responded to others had more pictures been shown.
span.quote: With respect to the number of concepts encoded by these neurons, even though many responsive neurons fired to a single concept, it cannot be ruled out that they could have responded to other concepts if more pictures were shown.

span.label: the selectivity estimates are explicitly upper bounds, because the images were personally relevant, about 100 pictures puts a floor of 1 percent on measurable selectivity, and still more selective neurons would be missed
span.quote: As a matter of fact, these estimates should only be considered as upper bounds, given that: (i) the images used were personally relevant to the subject, thus increasing the likelihood of eliciting a response; (ii) the relatively low number of pictures used (about 100) limits the lowest selectivity value to 1%; and (iii) it is difficult to detect very selective neurons firing to even fewer pictures, which are likely not presented in the ∼30-min recording sessions.

span.label: a unit firing to one concept may simply not have been shown the others, so single-concept responses cannot be taken as exclusive
span.quote: With respect to the number of concepts encoded by these neurons, even though many responsive neurons fired to a single concept, it cannot be ruled out that they could have responded to other concepts if more pictures were shown.

span.label: a further decay after many more repetitions cannot be excluded
span.quote: Although we cannot rule out a further decrease after many more repetitions, it seems that concept cells continue responding to a stimulus above baseline.

span.label: responses from sparsely firing or nearly silent neurons are commonly missed without optimal spike sorting
span.quote: The fact that responses from sparsely firing or nearly silent neurons can be missed without optimal spike sorting (Quian Quiroga, 2012a ; see also next section) is indeed a common finding with these recordings.

span.label: the degree of invariance seen in humans has not been matched in other animals, where the code is more distributed
span.quote: The high degree of visual invariance found in the human MTL has not been matched in other animals. In monkeys, the ITC shows a distributed code and limited robustness to basic image transformations

span.label: place cells as the comparison case for selectivity, fast learning, non-topographic organisation and firing without sensory input
span.quote: In addition, concept cells share many features with place cells in the rodent hippocampus (Quian Quiroga, 2012a ). Place cells increase their firing rate when the animal crosses a specific location in an environment (O’keefe & Nadel, 1978 ). They are selective, firing strongly to a particular place field, and they show fast learning, with its tuning being able to be formed within minutes (Wilson & McNaughton, 1993 ). They also show a non-topographic organization, in the sense that neighboring place fields do not correspond to nearby neurons

span.label: repetition suppression, imported as the expected shape of the response-versus-trial curve
span.quote: The screening data used in the study of Pedreira and colleagues had only six presentations of the stimuli. Although a response modulation with stimulus repetition was evident, the stability of these representations over several trials could not be addressed, as it was hard to see a steady state in the response strength. Therefore, the question of whether the response would end up reaching a baseline level after a sufficient number of repetitions remained open.

span.label: WHAT COUNTS AS A NEURON HERE IS A PRODUCT OF SORTING: the responsive units account for 4 and 1 percent of detected spikes, and one of the responses is invisible in the unsorted multiunit signal
span.quote: Throughout the 16-min recording, a total of 17 439 spikes was detected. However, these spikes belong to different units. In particular, clusters 3 and 5 are associated to single units that account for only 4% and 1% of the detected spikes, respectively. As shown in Fig. 3b , the unit in cluster 3 responds strongly to the picture of Vladimir Putin, with almost 20% of the spikes from this unit appearing between −500 and 1500 ms from the onset of this picture (representing 5% of the duration of the session). This response is more difficult to be visualized in the multiunit activity (i.e. just the detected spikes, without sorting). On the contrary, the response to the Taj Mahal from the unit in cluster 5, which also contains about 20% of the spikes from this unit, is not observed in the multiunit activity without the appropriate sorting.

span.label: so a whole class of objects - sparsely firing or nearly silent neurons - exists only if a particular processing choice is made, and the paper says missing them is a COMMON finding
span.quote: The fact that responses from sparsely firing or nearly silent neurons can be missed without optimal spike sorting (Quian Quiroga, 2012a ; see also next section) is indeed a common finding with these recordings.

span.label: THE STIMULUS SET SETS THE MEASUREMENT FLOOR: showing about 100 pictures makes 1 percent the smallest selectivity that can be observed, so the headline 1-3 percent figure is partly a property of the design
span.quote: As a matter of fact, these estimates should only be considered as upper bounds, given that: (i) the images used were personally relevant to the subject, thus increasing the likelihood of eliciting a response; (ii) the relatively low number of pictures used (about 100) limits the lowest selectivity value to 1%; and (iii) it is difficult to detect very selective neurons firing to even fewer pictures, which are likely not presented in the ∼30-min recording sessions.

span.label: and the picture set is tuned to each patient's own life and preferences, so selectivity figures from different subjects are not measurements of the same thing
span.quote: This set of pictures is actually tuned for each patient according to their preferences and background, as it has been shown that MTL neurons respond preferentially to personally relevant images

span.label: responsiveness is a three-part operational criterion, and the paper states the trade-off it was tuned against rather than presenting the thresholds as given
span.quote: After spikes were detected and sorted, it was necessary to quantitatively assess whether a particular unit responded to a particular picture. For this, we defined a responsiveness criterion that balanced the trade-off between false-positives and misses.

span.label: a concept cell is defined by INVARIANCE across pictures, written name and spoken name, not by responding to one image - which is what separates it from a visual feature detector
span.quote: The fact that these neurons fire to the concept represented by the stimulus and not to specific visual details, which could be common to a particular subset of pictures, is reinforced by the fact that the pictures of the same person used to test visual invariance included different backgrounds, poses, clothes, etc. More conclusive evidence of such conceptual representation is given by the fact that these neurons also fired to the written and spoken name of the person (or object) eliciting responses

span.label: replicates → Li et al. (1993); Pedreira et al. (2010)
span.quote: When looking at the first six trials, we observe a repetition suppression effect similar to the one reported in previous studies with stimulus-selective neurons (Li et al. 1993 ; Pedreira et al. 2010 ).

span.label: replicates → Pedreira et al. (2010)
span.quote: Confirming the findings of a previous study with a different dataset (Pedreira et al. 2010 ), we observe a decrease in the peak latency with trial number, which is related to a shortening of the response duration.

span.label: extends → Pedreira et al. (2010) and Li et al. (1993)
span.quote: A similar analysis was performed in Pedreira et al. ( 2010 ) and Li et al. ( 1993 ), but only using the first six repetitions.

span.label: extends → Pedreira 2010's repetition-suppression result in human MTL, which had only six presentations
span.quote: The screening data used in the study of Pedreira and colleagues had only six presentations of the stimuli. Although a response modulation with stimulus repetition was evident, the stability of these representations over several trials could not be addressed, as it was hard to see a steady state in the response strength. Therefore, the question of whether the response would end up reaching a baseline level after a sufficient number of repetitions remained open.

span.label: confirms → repetition suppression as described for stimulus-selective neurons in monkey inferotemporal cortex
span.quote: When looking at the first six trials, we observe a repetition suppression effect similar to the one reported in previous studies with stimulus-selective neurons (Li et al. 1993 ; Pedreira et al. 2010 ). For example, the decay of the response is well fitted by an exponential function. However, the larger number of repetitions used here lets us unveil that the response has a clear non-zero steady state, which is reached after ∼10 trials (as in Sawamura et al. 2006 ). In other words, although after several repetitions the response strength was smaller than in the first trial, it remained well above baseline even after about 30 repetitions, with about 15 intervening stimuli on average.

span.label: critiques → the grandmother-cell hypothesis of one neuron per concept
span.quote: The extreme case would be a one-to-one correspondence between a single neuron and a particular concept, leading to the so-called ‘grandmother cells’ (Quian Quiroga et al. 2008a , 2013 ). But there are several reasons to reject the hypothesis of having one single cell per concept.

span.label: qualifies → the inference from stimulus-recognition-dependent firing to a role for the MTL in conscious visual perception
span.quote: Given the vast amount of converging evidence supporting the role of the MTL in declarative memory processes but not in visual perception (Squire & Zola-Morgan, 1991 ; Eichenbaum, 2001 ; Squire et al. 2004 ; Moscovitch et al. 2005 ), it should be noted that this relationship between single-unit responses and stimulus recognition does not imply an involvement of the MTL in conscious visual perception.

span.label: builds-on → the original report of highly selective invariant concept cells in the human MTL
span.quote: The fact that these neurons fire to the concept represented by the stimulus and not to specific visual details, which could be common to a particular subset of pictures, is reinforced by the fact that the pictures of the same person used to test visual invariance included different backgrounds, poses, clothes, etc. More conclusive evidence of such conceptual representation is given by the fact that these neurons also fired to the written and spoken name of the person (or object) eliciting responses

span.quote: Throughout the 16-min recording, a total of 17 439 spikes was detected. However, these spikes belong to different units. In particular, clusters 3 and 5 are associated to single units that account for only 4% and 1% of the detected spikes, respectively. As shown in Fig. 3b , the unit in cluster 3 responds strongly to the picture of Vladimir Putin, with almost 20% of the spikes from this unit appearing between −500 and 1500 ms from the onset of this picture (representing 5% of the duration of the session). span.label: spike sorting —operationalised-as→ spike shapes
span.quote: The first step to process these recordings is to detect the spikes in the background noise (mainly generated by the activity of neurons further away), and to determine which spike corresponds to which neuron based on the spike shapes, a process called spike sorting (Quian Quiroga, 2012b ). For the data presented here, spike detection and sorting was performed using Wave_Clus (Quian Quiroga et al. 2004 ). Briefly, the steps typically involved in spike detection and sorting are: (i) band-pass filtering the data, for example between 300 and 3000 Hz, using a zero-phase filter to avoid distortion in the spike waveforms (Quian Quiroga, 2009 ); (ii) computation of a detection threshold based on a robust estimate of the noise statistics; (iii) feature extraction of the spike shapes, in the case of Wave_Clus using the wavelet transform; and (iv) clustering of the waveforms to identify the firing of the different units.

span.label: screening —operationalised-as→ pictures
span.quote: In order to find such stimuli, a simple visual task is used (Fig. 2 ), in which the subject is sat facing a laptop computer where a set of about 100 stimuli are presented for 1 s, six times each in pseudorandom order (Quian Quiroga et al. 2005 ). To make sure subjects pay attention to the stimuli, after the picture presentation they have to respond whether or not there was a person in the picture by pressing different arrow keys. These ‘screening sessions’ typically last about half an hour, and they are conducted in order to determine which neurons are responsive and to which set of pictures.

span.label: selectivity —operationalised-as→ pictures
span.quote: As a matter of fact, these estimates should only be considered as upper bounds, given that: (i) the images used were personally relevant to the subject, thus increasing the likelihood of eliciting a response; (ii) the relatively low number of pictures used (about 100) limits the lowest selectivity value to 1%; and (iii) it is difficult to detect very selective neurons firing to even fewer pictures, which are likely not presented in the ∼30-min recording sessions.

span.label: selectivity —operationalised-as→ MTL
span.quote: An important characteristic of these MTL neural responses is their high degree selectivity, with units responding on average only to 1–3% of the presented pictures

span.label: latency —operationalised-as→ MTL
span.quote: From the examples we have already presented, it can be seen that the MTL responses have a very precise onset, typically between 200 and 600 ms after stimulus onset, with a mean latency of about 300 ms

span.label: hippocampus —contrasted-with→ amygdala
span.quote: From the 441 channels analyzed in this study, 37% showed spiking activity from 457 units (either multi- or single-unit). After spikes were detected and sorted, it was necessary to quantitatively assess whether a particular unit responded to a particular picture. For this, we defined a responsiveness criterion that balanced the trade-off between false-positives and misses. According to our criterion, a responsive unit should fulfill the following conditions. First, in the response period (i.e. between 200 and 600 ms after stimulus onset) the unit should have a median number of spikes (across trials) larger than 1, to rule out neurons with too few spikes, and larger than μ b + 4 σ b , where μ b and σ b are the mean and standard deviation (across all stimuli) of the median number of spikes in the baseline period (between −600 and −200 ms). Second, it should have an average instantaneous firing rate (calculated by convolving the spike train with a Gaussian kernel) crossing over a threshold T for at least 100 ms (with the upwards and downwards crossings defining the spiking response onset and offset, respectively). The threshold T was set to μ FR + 4 σ FR , where μ FR and σ FR are the mean and standard deviation (across all stimuli) of the instantaneous firing rate during the baseline window (with a minimum at 5 Hz, for neurons with low baseline firing). Given that these MTL responses have a very well-defined onset (Mormann et al. 2008 ), this condition was introduced to avoid false-positive detections due to random increases spread over time. Third, to assure that the neuron’s response was consistent across trials, we compared the single-trial spike counts in the post-stimulus (200 ms, 600 ms) and baseline (−600 ms, −200 ms) windows with a paired sign test and required a significant difference with P < 0.01. Using this criterion, we identified a total of 72 responses (eight from amygdala and 64 from hippocampus), coming from 45 different units in 35 different channels.

In particular, clusters 3 and 5 are associated to single units that account for only 4% and 1% of the detected spikes, respectively. As shown in Fig. 3b , the unit in cluster 3 responds strongly to the picture of Vladimir Putin, with almost 20% of the spikes from this unit appearing between −500 and 1500 ms from the onset of this picture (representing 5% of the duration of the session). This response is more difficult to be visualized in the multiunit activity (i.e. just the detected spikes, without sorting). On the contrary, the response to the Taj Mahal from the unit in cluster 5, which also contains about 20% of the spikes from this unit, is not observed in the multiunit activity without the appropriate sorting.

span.label: and missing sparsely firing or nearly silent neurons without optimal sorting is stated to be a common finding
span.quote: The fact that responses from sparsely firing or nearly silent neurons can be missed without optimal spike sorting (Quian Quiroga, 2012a ; see also next section) is indeed a common finding with these recordings.

span.label: a second silent neuron, 2 percent of detected spikes, responded selectively to one picture and could not have been found without sorting
span.quote: Another example of a ‘silent neuron’ is shown in Fig. 4 , where cluster 3, which accounts for 2% of the spikes detected in this channel, is associated to a single unit selectively responding to a picture of George Harrison (this response accounts for 15% of the spikes from this unit, representing 3% of the duration of the session). As before, it would have been impossible to identify this response from the detected spikes without optimal spike sorting.

span.label: one cluster was left as multiunit because its signal-to-noise ratio did not permit separating the contributing cells
span.quote: Figure 4 shows also a multiunit cluster (cluster 1; i.e. a cluster where, due to low signal to noise ratio, it was not possible to separate the contribution of different units) that exhibits responses to a picture of the patient himself and to one of his daughter.

span.label: units respond on average to only 1 to 3 percent of presented pictures
span.quote: An important characteristic of these MTL neural responses is their high degree selectivity, with units responding on average only to 1–3% of the presented pictures

span.label: THE MEASUREMENT FLOOR IS THE DESIGN: the estimates are declared upper bounds because the images were personally relevant, about 100 pictures puts a floor of 1 percent on measurable selectivity, and more selective cells would be missed
span.quote: As a matter of fact, these estimates should only be considered as upper bounds, given that: (i) the images used were personally relevant to the subject, thus increasing the likelihood of eliciting a response; (ii) the relatively low number of pictures used (about 100) limits the lowest selectivity value to 1%; and (iii) it is difficult to detect very selective neurons firing to even fewer pictures, which are likely not presented in the ∼30-min recording sessions.

span.label: and a unit firing to one concept may simply not have been shown the others
span.quote: With respect to the number of concepts encoded by these neurons, even though many responsive neurons fired to a single concept, it cannot be ruled out that they could have responded to other concepts if more pictures were shown.

span.label: the picture set is tuned to each patient's own preferences and background, because personally relevant images are more likely to drive responses
span.quote: This set of pictures is actually tuned for each patient according to their preferences and background, as it has been shown that MTL neurons respond preferentially to personally relevant images

span.label: estimated fewer than a million of about a billion MTL neurons per concept, and 50 to 150 concepts per neuron
span.quote: Based on the total number of recorded neurons during a session, the number of stimuli presented and the number of responsive units, it has been estimated that out of about 10 9 MTL neurons, < 10 6 would be involved in representing a given concept (Waydo et al. 2006 ). Moreover, each MTL neuron was estimated to be involved in encoding between 50 and 150 distinct individuals or objects.

span.label: the one-cell-per-concept extreme is rejected while the small-assembly version is kept
span.quote: The extreme case would be a one-to-one correspondence between a single neuron and a particular concept, leading to the so-called ‘grandmother cells’ (Quian Quiroga et al. 2008a , 2013 ). But there are several reasons to reject the hypothesis of having one single cell per concept.

span.label: units firing to more than one concept are not uncommon, and neighbouring units encode unrelated concepts, suggesting non-topographic organisation
span.quote: In fact, it is not uncommon to find units that do fire to more than one concept (Quian Quiroga et al. 2005 , 2009 ). Such cases include responses to Jennifer Aniston and Lisa Kudrow (actresses of the series ‘Friends’), the Pisa and Eiffel towers (Quian Quiroga et al. 2005 ), Luke Skywalker and Yoda (Quian Quiroga et al. 2009 ), and Figs 4 and 6a in this work. At the same time, neighboring neurons (e.g. units recorded in the same channel and separated by performing spike sorting) are typically involved in encoding completely unrelated concepts (see Fig. 3 ; Quian Quiroga et al. 2009 ), which suggests a non-topographic organization.

span.label: RESPONSIVENESS IS A STATED TRADE-OFF: the criterion was defined to balance false positives against misses rather than presented as a given threshold
span.quote: After spikes were detected and sorted, it was necessary to quantitatively assess whether a particular unit responded to a particular picture. For this, we defined a responsiveness criterion that balanced the trade-off between false-positives and misses.

span.label: first condition: median spikes above one and above the baseline mean plus four standard deviations in a 200 to 600 ms window
span.quote: First, in the response period (i.e. between 200 and 600 ms after stimulus onset) the unit should have a median number of spikes (across trials) larger than 1, to rule out neurons with too few spikes, and larger than μ b + 4 σ b , where μ b and σ b are the mean and standard deviation (across all stimuli) of the median number of spikes in the baseline period (between −600 and −200 ms).

span.label: second condition: a sustained threshold crossing of at least 100 ms, added because a well-defined onset is expected and random scattered increases should not qualify
span.quote: Given that these MTL responses have a very well-defined onset (Mormann et al. 2008 ), this condition was introduced to avoid false-positive detections due to random increases spread over time.

span.label: third condition: a paired sign test on single-trial counts requiring consistency across trials at P below 0.01
span.quote: Third, to assure that the neuron’s response was consistent across trials, we compared the single-trial spike counts in the post-stimulus (200 ms, 600 ms) and baseline (−600 ms, −200 ms) windows with a paired sign test and required a significant difference with P < 0.01.

span.label: 37 percent of 441 channels carried spiking activity, yielding 72 responses from 45 units
span.quote: From the 441 channels analyzed in this study, 37% showed spiking activity from 457 units (either multi- or single-unit). After spikes were detected and sorted, it was necessary to quantitatively assess whether a particular unit responded to a particular picture. For this, we defined a responsiveness criterion that balanced the trade-off between false-positives and misses. According to our criterion, a responsive unit should fulfill the following conditions. First, in the response period (i.e. between 200 and 600 ms after stimulus onset) the unit should have a median number of spikes (across trials) larger than 1, to rule out neurons with too few spikes, and larger than μ b + 4 σ b , where μ b and σ b are the mean and standard deviation (across all stimuli) of the median number of spikes in the baseline period (between −600 and −200 ms). Second, it should have an average instantaneous firing rate (calculated by convolving the spike train with a Gaussian kernel) crossing over a threshold T for at least 100 ms (with the upwards and downwards crossings defining the spiking response onset and offset, respectively). The threshold T was set to μ FR + 4 σ FR , where μ FR and σ FR are the mean and standard deviation (across all stimuli) of the instantaneous firing rate during the baseline window (with a minimum at 5 Hz, for neurons with low baseline firing). Given that these MTL responses have a very well-defined onset (Mormann et al. 2008 ), this condition was introduced to avoid false-positive detections due to random increases spread over time. Third, to assure that the neuron’s response was consistent across trials, we compared the single-trial spike counts in the post-stimulus (200 ms, 600 ms) and baseline (−600 ms, −200 ms) windows with a paired sign test and required a significant difference with P < 0.01. Using this criterion, we identified a total of 72 responses (eight from amygdala and 64 from hippocampus), coming from 45 different units in 35 different channels.

span.label: invariance extends beyond pictures to the written and spoken name of the same person, which is what makes the response conceptual rather than visual
span.quote: The fact that these neurons fire to the concept represented by the stimulus and not to specific visual details, which could be common to a particular subset of pictures, is reinforced by the fact that the pictures of the same person used to test visual invariance included different backgrounds, poses, clothes, etc. More conclusive evidence of such conceptual representation is given by the fact that these neurons also fired to the written and spoken name of the person (or object) eliciting responses

span.label: identity could be decoded from the firing but not which picture of that person was shown
span.quote: Given the selectivity of these responses, the firing of these neurons was used to decode the identity of the person being shown, but it was in general not possible to decode which picture of the person was presented each time (Quian Quiroga et al. 2007 ). Therefore, these neurons give an explicit representation of the meaning of the stimuli (i.e. the neuron tells who the person being shown is).

span.label: responses can be internally generated: imagining a picture produced the same selective firing as seeing it
span.quote: Another feature of these MTL responses is that they can be internally generated in the absence of the physical stimulus. When subjects imagined pictures that previously triggered the firing of a neuron (i.e. without the actual visual stimulus being shown), it was possible to see the same selective response as when viewing the picture

span.label: response likelihood is ordered by personal relevance: family and experimenters, then celebrities, then unfamiliar faces
span.quote: In line, it has been shown that pictures of family members, including pictures of the patients themselves (see Fig. 4b ), and pictures of the researchers performing experiments with the patients, who are in close contact with them throughout their stay in hospital, are the most likely to elicit responses, followed by pictures of celebrities, and then by pictures of unfamiliar faces (Viskontas et al. 2009 ). In other words, we can infer that the more personally relevant the stimulus, the larger the number of neurons encoding it.

span.label: A GUARD AGAINST AN OVER-READING: recognition-dependent firing does not imply the MTL is involved in conscious visual perception
span.quote: Given the vast amount of converging evidence supporting the role of the MTL in declarative memory processes but not in visual perception (Squire & Zola-Morgan, 1991 ; Eichenbaum, 2001 ; Squire et al. 2004 ; Moscovitch et al. 2005 ), it should be noted that this relationship between single-unit responses and stimulus recognition does not imply an involvement of the MTL in conscious visual perception.

span.label: responses begin 200 to 600 ms after stimulus onset with a mean near 300 ms, well after inferotemporal responses
span.quote: From the examples we have already presented, it can be seen that the MTL responses have a very precise onset, typically between 200 and 600 ms after stimulus onset, with a mean latency of about 300 ms

span.label: interneurons classified by spike width and firing rate fire to more stimuli, suggesting a winner-take-all sharpening step
span.quote: First of all, on the basis of their spike widths and firing rates it is in principle possible to classify neurons as interneurons or pyramidal cells. Using this classification, it was reported that MTL interneurons tend to fire to a larger number of stimuli, a finding that suggests a winner-takes-all mechanism that (by suppressing the firing of other neurons) may generate the very selective responses of pyramidal cells

span.label: concept cells share selectivity, fast learning, non-topographic organisation and stimulus-free firing with rodent place cells
span.quote: In addition, concept cells share many features with place cells in the rodent hippocampus (Quian Quiroga, 2012a ). Place cells increase their firing rate when the animal crosses a specific location in an environment (O’keefe & Nadel, 1978 ). They are selective, firing strongly to a particular place field, and they show fast learning, with its tuning being able to be formed within minutes (Wilson & McNaughton, 1993 ). They also show a non-topographic organization, in the sense that neighboring place fields do not correspond to nearby neurons

span.label: the degree of invariance has not been matched in other animals, where inferotemporal coding is distributed and less transformation-robust
span.quote: The high degree of visual invariance found in the human MTL has not been matched in other animals. In monkeys, the ITC shows a distributed code and limited robustness to basic image transformations

span.quote: The first step to process these recordings is to detect the spikes in the background noise (mainly generated by the activity of neurons further away), and to determine which spike corresponds to which neuron based on the spike shapes, a process called spike sorting (Quian Quiroga, 2012b ). For the data presented here, spike detection and sorting was performed using Wave_Clus (Quian Quiroga et al. 2004 ). Briefly, the steps typically involved in spike detection and sorting are: (i) band-pass filtering the data, for example between 300 and 3000 Hz, using a zero-phase filter to avoid distortion in the spike waveforms (Quian Quiroga, 2009 ); (ii) computation of a detection threshold based on a robust estimate of the noise statistics; (iii) feature extraction of the spike shapes, in the case of Wave_Clus using the wavelet transform; and (iv) clustering of the waveforms to identify the firing of the different units.
